phases.title: Foundation
phases.goal: Conceptual clarity in the maths-heavy subjects.
activities: Solve previous-year questions topic by topic as each topic is finished.
Build a formula sheet while studying, not at the end.

phases.title: Core CS
activities: One formula and concept sheet per subject.
Keep a running list of weak areas.

phases.title: Revision and mocks
phases.goal: Rapid full-syllabus revision and the first full-length mocks.
activities: Revise the whole syllabus quickly, subject by subject.
Analyse every mock: wrong answers and time spent.
Reinforce the weak areas the mocks expose.

phases.title: Intensive mock drills
activities: Two to three full mocks per week.
Full previous-year papers from the last ten years.
Final formula sheets and mental shortcuts.

targetScore.text: 70–75+ marks is the usual planning target for a top-100 rank; the real cut-off moves with each year's paper.

strategy.text: MSQ and NAT questions carry no negative marking, so never leave one blank: any answer beats an empty box.
An MCQ guess pays off on average once the chance of being right exceeds 25%, for 1-mark and 2-mark questions alike. Eliminating one option of four already gets you there (1 in 3).
A blind guess on a four-option MCQ has an expected score of exactly zero: it adds risk, not marks. Guess only after eliminating something.
Take the 1-mark questions in a first pass for time, not risk: they are quicker per mark, and the MCQ penalty is a third of the question's marks either way.
On a 2-mark question that is not yielding, mark it for review and move on; come back with the time you saved.
Use the virtual calculator for arithmetic you would otherwise do twice; it is slow, so do the reasoning first and the arithmetic once.

traps.text: Calculation slips in numericals: write neatly and recheck the arithmetic.
Misreading the question's polarity: "is / is not", "always / never", "which is FALSE".
Off-by-one errors in loop counts and complexity.
Missing base cases or boundary conditions in dynamic programming.
Careless FIRST and FOLLOW set computation.
Forgetting stall cycles in pipeline hazard questions.
Mixing up physical and virtual addresses in memory questions.

errata.claim: Negative marking: −1/3 for 1-mark and −2/3 for 2-mark questions.
errata.correction: The penalty applies to MCQs only. MSQ and NAT questions have no negative marking (and no partial credit).

errata.claim: Attempt a 1-mark question when the probability of being correct exceeds 50%, a 2-mark question above 40%, because the expected value is then positive.
errata.correction: The expected value turns positive at 25% for both: p − (1 − p)/3 > 0 and 2p − 2(1 − p)/3 > 0 both reduce to p > 1/4. For MSQ and NAT any attempt is free.

errata.claim: Do the 1-mark questions first because their negative-marking risk-to-reward ratio is lower.
errata.correction: The ratio is identical: a wrong MCQ costs one third of its marks whether it carries 1 or 2. Doing 1-mark questions first is a time strategy.

errata.claim: Never guess blindly; negative marking hurts the score significantly.
errata.correction: A blind guess on a four-option MCQ has an expected score of 0 (¼ × 1 − ¾ × ⅓), so it adds variance rather than losing marks on average; on MSQ and NAT a guess can only help.

errata.claim: Time split: GA 25–30 minutes, CS 150–155 minutes, review 15–20 minutes.
errata.correction: That adds up to 190–205 minutes against the 180 available. A split that fits is GA about 25, CS about 140 and review about 15 minutes.
